text.en: FADE IN:

A tidy farmhouse at the edge of a wide meadow. MOTHER PIG stands in the doorway as three young PIGS shoulder their sacks: FIRST PIG, already yawning; SECOND PIG, humming a tune under his breath; THIRD PIG, checking a folded sketch of a house plan against the morning light.
You're all old enough now to build a place of your own. Choose well, and mind the wolf that's been seen past the millpond.
(rolling his eyes)
Everyone's always minding that wolf. I've never even seen him.
That's rather the point of minding him.
(folding the sketch away)
I'll mind him. Whatever it costs in time.
Spoken like someone who's going to be building all week while the rest of us are settled in by supper.
Mother Pig kisses each of them on the snout and watches them set off down three different paths, waving until the meadow grass swallows them from view.
The three pigs pause where the paths split, sacks over their shoulders.
There's a whole field of straw not a mile off. I'll have four walls up by noon.
I saw a stand of good sticks near the old orchard. Sturdier than straw, and hardly slower.
And I saw the brickworks by the crossroads, if either of you change your minds before it's too late to matter.
(already walking)
Bricks. Honestly. Whoever finishes first wins, agreed?
Finishing isn't the same as finishing well.
They part ways down three different paths.

Golden straw stretches in every direction. First Pig works quickly, tying bundle after bundle, humming the same tune his brother started that morning. By midday, four walls and a roof stand assembled, leaning ever so slightly in the breeze.
(admiring it, hands on hips)
Good enough for a nap, at least. And no one said it had to last forever.
He drags his sack of belongings inside, arranges a stool by the window, and settles in with visible satisfaction.

Second Pig works with more care, weaving sticks into a lattice frame, tying each joint twice before moving to the next. The sun climbs higher. By late afternoon, a small but respectable stick house stands among the apple trees.
(stepping back to admire it)
There. Not bricks, but it'll turn a strong wind, at least.
He's barely finished the sentence when FIRST PIG comes pelting down the orchard path, out of breath, sack bouncing against his back.
Wolf! Wolf right behind me - my house is gone, just gone, in one breath!
(already pulling him toward the door)
In. Quickly.
They duck inside just as a shape appears at the far end of the orchard path - unhurried, sniffing the air with evident interest.
The two pigs press against the far wall as a shadow falls across the doorway. A polite knock follows, oddly formal given the circumstances.
Little pigs, little pigs, won't you let me in?
(through the door, doing his best to sound calm)
Not by the hair of our chinny chin chins.
Then I'll huff, and I'll puff, and I'll blow your house in.
A pause. Then a great inward breath, audible even through the walls.

The stick walls groan, crack along every woven joint, and collapse outward in a cloud of splinters and loose apples shaken from the nearest tree. Both pigs are already sprinting toward a distant chimney, visible above the tree line.
A solid, handsome brick house stands at the crossroads, chimney smoking gently. THIRD PIG sets the last brick of a garden wall in place, steps back, and allows himself a small, satisfied nod.
In the distance, two shapes come tearing across the field toward him, and behind them, a third shape, larger, loping unhurried.
(already moving to the door)
That'll be them, then. Later than I'd hoped, but no matter.
He opens the door before the other two even reach the gate. They tumble inside, gasping. The door bolts shut behind them with a solid, reassuring click.
(catching his breath)
Two houses. Two houses, gone, just like that.
I told you sticks would turn a strong wind. I didn't account for whatever that was.
(calmly setting a kettle on the stove)
Bricks account for a great deal more than either of you gave them credit for this morning.
A polite knock sounds at the door. The Wolf, a little winded from the chase but composed, eyes the solid brick walls with noticeably less enthusiasm than before.
Little pigs, little pigs, won't you let me in?
(calm, through the door)
Not by the hair of our chinny chin chins.
Then I'll huff, and I'll puff -

He huffs. The windows rattle faintly and nothing more. He puffs again, longer this time. The bricks do not move even slightly. A third attempt leaves him audibly out of breath, and a long silence follows.
(at the window, daring a look)
He's sitting down. In the garden. Thinking.
Let him think. It won't get him through a brick wall.
The Wolf sits back on his haunches in the garden, considering the chimney with narrowed eyes. After a long moment, he rises, circles the house once, and begins climbing the ivy toward the roof.
A scrabbling sound crosses the roof overhead, moving toward the chimney. Third Pig looks up, unsurprised.
Get the pot. The big one, from under the sink.
(already moving)
You knew he'd try the chimney?
I built the chimney knowing someone might.

They swing a large pot of water over the hearth fire and step well back. Above, the scrabbling grows louder, then stops entirely - just before a shower of soot and one very surprised Wolf comes down the flue in a rush.
He lands in the pot with an enormous splash, yelps loud enough to rattle the windows, and is out the door and across the crossroads before any of the three pigs can find a single word to say.
The three pigs stand in the doorway, watching the Wolf's dwindling shape vanish over the far hill and not come back.
So. Bricks, then.
(folding his arms, not quite smiling)
Bricks, then.
(already eyeing the garden wall)
Any chance you'd help me build a proper house before winter?
On one condition - you listen to the whole plan this time, start to finish.
Start to finish. I promise.
The kettle whistles. Three pigs sit around a small table, mugs in hand, the pot that saved them still cooling by the hearth, sooty and dented and entirely unwilling to be put away just yet.
(raising his mug)
To bricks, and to whoever's idea they were.
(raising his in return)
To listening the first time, next time.
(grinning over the rim of his own mug)
Let's not get carried away.
FADE OUT.
